# Need for Closure and Misinformation Acceptance: A Small, Conditional Effect

Need for cognitive closure appears to have a small, context-dependent relationship with accepting some misinformation, especially when situations are ambiguous and a simple explanation is readily available. It is not established as a general cause: a Polish memory study found a small positive association, and a German panel found a small association with COVID-19 conspiracy beliefs, but a fully adjusted Hungarian fake-news study found no need-for-closure effect, while a seven-study illusory-truth program found no moderation by closure. No supplied study directly randomized need for closure and then measured misinformation belief, credibility, sharing, or correction acceptance. Confidence is therefore moderate for a conditional association and low for a uniform or causal effect.

The analysis proceeds in six steps. It first defines need for closure and separates belief, credibility, memory, sharing, correction, and accuracy outcomes. It then weighs positive, null, and negative findings; explains proposed mechanisms; examines uncertainty, threat, ideology, source cues, time pressure, platforms, and corrections; compares closure with related predictors; and closes with limitations and practical implications.

## 1. Constructs and outcome definitions

### What need for closure means

Need for cognitive closure is the desire for definite knowledge and the avoidance of confusion and ambiguity. Webster and Kruglanski describe it as a graded motive: its strength depends on how beneficial closure seems and how costly uncertainty feels in a particular situation, while people also differ in their stable tendency to value closure. The theory distinguishes “urgency”—seizing an early answer—from “permanence”—freezing on and protecting an answer already reached ([Webster and Kruglanski’s review](https://doi.org/10.1080/14792779643000100)).

This definition matters because need for closure is not the same as wanting a true answer. It is a desire to end uncertainty, potentially by accepting the first sufficiently plausible account. That account could be accurate, inaccurate, official, conspiratorial, or politically congenial. The predicted risk is therefore not necessarily “more false beliefs” in every setting; it is faster commitment and less willingness to continue searching when the available answer is misleading.

Need for closure can be measured as a relatively stable disposition or examined as a situational state. Trait measures include the original 32-item Need for Closure Scale and shortened 15-item and five-item versions. Situational closure can be heightened by conditions such as time pressure, cognitive load, noisy environments, or threat; accountability and accuracy demands can reduce the willingness to settle quickly. The distinction is important because a person with a generally moderate need for closure may nevertheless seek certainty urgently during a crisis.

The measures used in the misinformation-related evidence are not identical:

| Study or context | Closure measure | Reliability or qualification |
|---|---|---|
| Hejniak et al. | 15-item shortened scale, five dimensions | α = .74; included ambiguity discomfort, order, predictability, closed-mindedness, and decisiveness |
| Polish COVID-19 study | 15-item scale, rated 1–6 | Subscale α values ranged from .56 to .78, with especially low reliability for ambiguity avoidance and closed-mindedness |
| German panel | Five-item NFCS | α = .67 |
| U.S. COVID-19 study | 15-item need-for-closure scale | The supplied results do not provide its closure-specific coefficient |
| Warning-tag study | NFCC included among individual-difference predictors | The abstract reports significant influence on tag attitudes and self-described behavior but gives no direction or effect size |

The variation makes direct comparison difficult. Short scales are efficient but may measure somewhat different mixtures of certainty seeking, decisiveness, order preference, and closed-mindedness. A 2026 Turkish validation removed three closed-mindedness items from a 15-item short form because their factor loadings were below .40, arguing that openness to different ideas should not automatically be equated with the need for certainty ([Yavuzalp and Bahcivan](https://un-pub.eu/ojs/index.php/gjpr/article/view/9950/10480)). Cross-cultural validation likewise found structural invariance but only partial metric and scalar invariance across Polish, Flemish, Korean, and American samples ([Psychologica Belgica validation study](https://psychologicabelgica.com/articles/10.5334/pb.998)). The construct is broadly comparable across settings, but mean scores and subscale meanings should not be treated as perfectly interchangeable.

### What counts as misinformation acceptance

“Misinformation” generally means information that is false, inaccurate, or misleading. “Fake news” is a narrower and contested term often referring to false content presented in a news-like format; it should not be treated as synonymous with every form of misinformation ([Ross, Rand, and Pennycook](https://www.sas.upenn.edu/~baron/journal/20/200616b/jdm200616b.html); [Behavioral Sciences terminology review](https://doi.org/10.3390/bs16071112)).

Acceptance is also not one outcome. Research has measured at least six related but distinct responses:

| Outcome | What it measures | Why it matters |
|---|---|---|
| Direct belief or endorsement | Whether a person rates a false claim as probably or definitely true | Closest to ordinary “acceptance,” but often self-reported |
| Perceived credibility | Whether a post, source, or article seems trustworthy | Can change without changing explicit belief |
| Memory susceptibility | Whether misleading details enter later recall | Shows misinformation effects without proving conscious endorsement |
| Inference or reasoning | Whether a person draws conclusions consistent with a false claim | May reveal indirect influence even when direct belief is unchanged |
| Sharing or behavioral acceptance | Willingness or intention to forward content | Does not prove that the person believes it |
| Correction acceptance and continued influence | Whether a person revises belief or continues reasoning from a corrected claim | A separate post-exposure process |

For example, Hejniak et al. measured memory for misleading details, not news credibility. The U.S. COVID-19 study measured endorsement of myth-busting items, not sharing. A correction study measured both claim-congruent inferences and direct belief, and obtained different results for the two. A social-media experiment measured sharing likelihood and found that a fact-check alert reduced sharing, but the authors explicitly noted that an alert need not stop people from trusting the content ([Nekmat’s fact-check-alert experiment](https://doi.org/10.1177/2056305119897322)).

Consequently, evidence that closure predicts memory distortion cannot automatically be described as evidence that it causes belief in fake news. Evidence that it predicts sharing intention cannot automatically be described as evidence that a person accepted the claim. The central question must always specify which form of acceptance is under discussion.

## 2. What the evidence shows

### The strongest positive findings are small and conditional

The clearest positive result comes from a 2019 Polish study by Hejniak and colleagues. In its first experiment, 174 psychology undergraduates and high-school students watched a silent-film robbery and later answered open-ended memory questions after receiving a description containing six misleading details. Among participants exposed to misinformation, those classified as high in need for cognitive closure gave more misinformation-consistent responses than those classified as low in closure: the means were 1.84 versus 1.36, with *F*(1,162) = 5.30, *p* = .023, η² = .03. The correlation between closure and susceptibility was *r*(133) = .25, *p* = .002 ([Hejniak et al.](https://arch.ies.gov.pl/images/PDF/2019/vol_118/118_Hejniak_m.pdf)).

The effect is small. The η² value indicates that approximately 3% of variance in that group comparison was associated with the closure grouping, and the correlation is a modest bivariate relationship rather than a causal estimate. Closure was measured rather than manipulated, and the sample was young, voluntary, and drawn from educational settings. Most importantly, the outcome was memory susceptibility after misleading information, not a direct rating that a false news claim was credible.

The same paper illustrates why the relationship should not be treated as uniformly positive. In a second experiment involving a false-confession paradigm, 87% of 103 participants signed a false-guilt declaration, but high-closure participants did not sign more often than low-closure participants (*p* = .674). The authors reported a small overall association with coerced-compliant confession, but the more direct high-versus-low comparison did not support the expected difference. This adjacent result suggests that a closure motive may matter differently depending on whether the outcome is memory, compliance, belief, or behavior.

A larger and more representative positive finding comes from a German multiwave panel study. Need for closure was measured before the COVID-19 pandemic, while participants later rated the likelihood of three COVID-19 conspiracy claims: that the virus was a biological weapon, that it was being used to restrict civil rights and begin surveillance, and that its danger and spread were deliberately exaggerated. Among 2,883 German respondents, closure correlated with conspiracy acceptance at *r* = .12. In a covariate-adjusted model with 2,491 cases, the coefficient was *B* = .08, with a 95% confidence interval of [.04, .11]. The authors characterized the association as small ([Jedinger and Masch](https://www.frontiersin.org/journals/social-psychology/articles/10.3389/frsps.2024.1447313/full)).

This study improves on the Polish study in population coverage and temporal separation, but it remains correlational. The two measurements were collected at different times, which helps establish ordering but does not rule out stable third variables or selective exposure. The outcome was likelihood-rated endorsement of three conspiracy narratives, not general misinformation discernment, social-media sharing, or correction acceptance.

The German study also shows that closure was not the dominant predictor in that setting. Political trust had a coefficient of *B* = −.33, and crisis-specific trust had *B* = −.51, both substantially larger in magnitude than the closure coefficient. The preregistered interactions between closure and political trust or crisis trust were approximately zero, so the proposed moderation was not supported. Closure was associated with conspiracy acceptance across trust levels, but trust did not determine when the closure relationship appeared.

A Polish COVID-19 study offers a related but less direct result. In an online snowball sample of 380 adults surveyed in September and October 2020, need-for-closure subdimensions were related to conspiracy belief and coronavirus fear. The outcome combined agreement with 10 factual claims, 10 opinions, and 10 conspiracy theories, so it was not a pure misinformation measure. The structural model explained only 3% of the variance in conspiracy belief; avoidance of ambiguity and closed-mindedness were positively associated with conspiracy belief, while predictability showed a different pattern. The authors reported indirect paths through conspiracy belief, but the survey was observational and cannot establish causal mediation ([Polish COVID-19 study](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9690611/)).

These findings support a cautious proposition: closure may make some people more receptive to a certainty-producing explanation when information is confusing or threatening. They do not support the stronger proposition that need for closure reliably makes people believe false information.

### Null and counterevidence is substantial

The most important counterexample is a Hungarian study conducted in a politically polarized context. Its fully adjusted regressions controlled for demographics, political knowledge, scientific literacy, political interest, political orientation, right-wing authoritarianism, system justification, conspiracy mentality, and social dominance orientation. Need for closure was effectively zero for belief in pro-government fake news: *B* = .002, β = .001, *t* = .022. It was also nonsignificant for pro-government real news: *B* = −.037, β = −.024, *t* = −.430. A bivariate closure correlation with belief in pro-government real news was *r* = .12, but that association disappeared under adjustment ([Szebeni, Lönnqvist, and Jasinskaja-Lahti](https://www.frontiersin.org/journals/psychology/articles/10.3389/fpsyg.2021.790848/full)).

In that study, conspiracy mentality was the only psychological predisposition consistently associated with belief in political and nonpolitical fake news. Political orientation predicted greater belief when the news matched participants’ political identity, while political interest was associated with better discrimination between real and fake political news. The result challenges the idea that closure is a distinctive or robust predictor once more content-specific and political variables are included.

The Hungarian design also removed source information from every news item. That controlled away source credibility, but it means the study could not test the possibility that high-closure participants rely especially strongly on source cues. A null result in a source-free task does not prove that closure would be irrelevant when a trusted authority, familiar brand, partisan messenger, or social-endorsement cue is present.

A seven-study investigation of the illusory-truth effect provides another boundary. Across seven studies with a combined sample of 2,196, participants were more likely to judge previously encountered statements as true. The materials included trivia claims and partisan news headlines. Yet the studies found no evidence that need for cognitive closure or other cognitive measures moderated the repetition effect. Closure was directly examined as an individual-difference moderator in one study, not manipulated, but the overall result still contradicts the prediction that high closure universally magnifies familiarity-based acceptance ([De Keersmaecker et al.](https://doi.org/10.1177/0146167219853844)).

An earlier United Kingdom study also found near-zero correlations between need for cognitive closure and both real-world conspiracy beliefs and attribution of a conspiracy to a fictitious event: *r* = −.05 for each outcome in a sample of only 30 undergraduates. In a second study with 86 students, an accountability procedure intended to lower closure reduced the influence of participants’ prior conspiracy beliefs on judgments about a fictitious political event. This is suggestive of a conditional effect, but the sample was small, the event was hypothetical, and the outcome was not ordinary misinformation acceptance. It is better interpreted as adjacent experimental evidence that closure can affect how prior beliefs are used than as a direct causal test of fake-news belief ([Frontiers in Psychology study](https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2013.00378)).

Recent work on misinformation warning tags is relevant but incomplete. A 2025 ACM study combined 132 Amazon Mechanical Turk participants and 112 undergraduates. It reported that attitudes toward warning tags and self-described behaviors were influenced by need for cognitive closure, political orientation, and trust in medical scientists after covariate adjustment. The abstract does not report the direction or magnitude of the closure effect, and the outcome concerns attitudes toward tags rather than a direct test of whether closure increases false belief ([warning-tag study](https://dl.acm.org/doi/10.1145/3757521)). It is promising evidence that closure may matter for intervention reception, but it cannot resolve the central causal question.

### What can be concluded about effect size and causality?

The strongest supported quantitative conclusion is that observed positive associations are small. The Polish memory study reports η² = .03 and *r* = .25. The German panel reports *r* = .12 and an adjusted coefficient of .08. There is no focused pooled effect size for need for closure and misinformation acceptance in the supplied evidence, and the outcomes are too heterogeneous to treat these values as interchangeable.

The causal evidence is weaker still. None of the core misinformation studies directly randomized a trait or situational manipulation of need for closure and then measured belief, credibility, sharing, or correction acceptance. The Polish and German positive findings are correlational. The Polish mediation model is observational. The UK accountability study manipulated or purported to manipulate closure in an adjacent conspiracy-judgment task, not a standard misinformation paradigm. The evidence therefore supports a plausible association, not a demonstrated causal pathway.

The most defensible judgment is that high need for closure can contribute to misinformation acceptance under some conditions, but it is neither necessary nor sufficient. Many people with high closure will reject misinformation, and many people with low closure may accept it for reasons involving identity, trust, familiarity, ignorance, emotion, or social incentives.

## 3. How need for closure may influence acceptance

### Closure can shorten information search

The most established mechanism is not “believing falsehoods” but stopping the search for evidence. High closure creates pressure to reach a definite answer. If a simple cue is available, the person may seize it; once the answer feels adequate, permanence or freezing makes further reconsideration less likely.

Klein and Webster’s experiments on persuasive messages found that people high in dispositional need for closure relied on heuristic cues and failed to scrutinize message content systematically. When no convenient heuristic cue was available, however, high-closure participants processed more systematically. This conditional pattern is central: closure does not inevitably produce shallow processing. It increases reliance on the easiest available route to certainty ([Klein and Webster](https://doi.org/10.1207/s15324834basp2202_5)).

Applied to misinformation, the implication is straightforward but not yet directly proven. A headline, source logo, confident spokesperson, repeated phrase, or group endorsement can provide an easy basis for a judgment. If that cue points toward a false claim, high closure may encourage early acceptance. If it points toward accurate information, the same motive may produce rapid acceptance of truth. Closure is therefore expected to amplify dependence on available cues rather than selectively favor falsehood.

This also explains why source-free designs are limited. The Hungarian study deliberately removed sources to eliminate source effects. That was useful for estimating content-based judgments, but it prevented researchers from testing whether closure changes reliance on authority, familiarity, or institutional reputation.

### Accessible misinformation may become an anchor

Hejniak et al. proposed a more specific mechanism for their memory findings. When original information conflicts with later misleading information, the conflict creates uncertainty. The misleading detail may be more recent and more accessible, making it an “anchoring point” around which a high-closure participant organizes an answer. Once the anchor supplies enough certainty, memory search may stop rather than continue toward the original detail ([Hejniak et al.](https://arch.ies.gov.pl/images/PDF/2019/vol_118/118_Hejniak_m.pdf)).

This interpretation fits the urgency–permanence model. Urgency favors the accessible answer; permanence protects the answer after it has been adopted. But the study did not measure the proposed steps separately. There was no mediation test of uncertainty, anchoring, retrieval, or search termination, and the experiment did not manipulate closure. The mechanism is plausible interpretation, not established causal evidence.

It also concerns memory rather than credibility. A participant might reproduce a misleading detail because it is easy to retrieve without consciously believing a false news story. That is why memory susceptibility should not be silently converted into “misinformation acceptance.”

### Conspiracy narratives can supply a stable explanation

Conspiracy narratives are especially relevant because they often convert a confusing event into a coherent story with identifiable agents, motives, and causes. The German study describes high closure as promoting “seizing” on a need-satisfying explanation and “freezing” on it. The Polish COVID-19 paper similarly proposes that conspiracy narratives can provide a stable framework and a sense of familiarity during an uncertain crisis.

Threat research outside misinformation provides causal support for the first part of this chain. Thórisdóttir and Jost reported across several studies that threat increased motivated closed-mindedness, and that closed-mindedness mediated a shift toward political conservatism. Their work shows that threat can change closure-related cognition; it does not show that threat makes people accept misinformation, nor that conspiratorial claims are the inevitable result ([Thórisdóttir and Jost](https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1111/j.1467-9221.2011.00840.x)).

The Polish COVID-19 study provides a closer but still observational link. Some closure subdimensions were related to conspiracy belief, and conspiracy belief was statistically connected to coronavirus fear. Yet the model explained little variance in conspiracy belief, and the direction of the fear relationship was not a simple “more fear causes more conspiracy belief” pattern. People can endorse conspiracies because they feel threatened, but they can also use conspiracy explanations to reduce or organize threat. The causal ordering remains unresolved.

### Repetition and familiarity operate broadly, not specifically through closure

Repeated exposure can make claims feel familiar, and familiarity can be misread as truth. This illusory-truth effect is robust across many studies and materials. However, the seven-study program found no closure moderation, so repetition alone does not establish a special vulnerability among people high in need for closure ([De Keersmaecker et al.](https://doi.org/10.1177/0146167219853844)).

Correction research further shows why the mechanism should be handled carefully. Three online experiments with a total of 1,718 participants tested whether corrections introducing novel false claims would create familiarity backfire after a one-week delay. Overall, corrections did not produce stronger misconceptions than a no-exposure control. In one experiment, fact-check-only exposure slightly increased false-claim inference scores relative to no exposure: *M* = 5.40 versus 5.06, ηp² = .014. But direct false-claim belief did not differ: *M* = 4.39 versus 4.38. The inference effect therefore did not generalize to explicit belief ([Cognitive Research correction study](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s41235-020-00241-6)).

The general mechanism—repetition increases fluency and retrieval—is well established enough to inform communication, but its NFC-specific form is not. The evidence does not show that high-closure people are uniquely affected by repetition or that they are especially prone to familiarity backfire.

### Source cues and social endorsement can replace content scrutiny

When information is complicated, people commonly use source cues, social endorsement, professionalism, or familiarity as shortcuts. Need for closure may make such cues more attractive when they offer a rapid path to a definite judgment. Yet the supplied evidence does not contain a direct test of need for closure as a mediator between source cues and misinformation acceptance.

Broader misinformation research shows why this possibility matters. In a Chinese online experiment with 481 social-media users, social-endorsement cues and the slant of news content affected both veracity judgments and online engagement. Participants generally showed a truth bias and were better at identifying truthful than false news, while evidence about epistemic motive and deliberative thinking was mixed ([Yan and Pan](https://doi.org/10.1080/15213269.2023.2208363)).

A Singapore experiment with 929 participants found that fact-check alerts reduced intended sharing, but the reduction depended on source. Sharing likelihood was lower for unfamiliar non-mainstream news overall, yet the alert produced a larger decrease for mainstream news. Media skepticism did not significantly moderate the full alert-by-source interaction, although within the mainstream-source group, alert effects varied with skepticism. These results show that source and intervention cues can shape sharing without demonstrating an NFC effect ([Nekmat](https://doi.org/10.1177/2056305119897322)).

The practical implication is that a high-closure person may be especially responsive to whichever source cue appears most decisive, but that remains a hypothesis. It could produce trust in a reputable correction, trust in a familiar misinformation source, or distrust of both if the cue conflicts with identity.

### Motivated reasoning is a possible amplifier, not an NFC-specific finding

Need for closure may interact with motivated reasoning by encouraging people to settle on information that fits an existing worldview. Once a conclusion is reached, the permanence tendency may make contrary evidence feel disruptive. But political identity and motivated reasoning are not synonyms for need for closure.

The Hungarian study found that political orientation predicted belief in political news when content matched identity, including both fake and real news. A review of misinformation research likewise concludes that motivated reasoning can operate among liberals and conservatives, rather than supporting a simple partisan stereotype ([Social Media and Democracy review](https://www.cambridge.org/core/books/social-media-and-democracy/misinformation-and-its-correction/61FA7FD743784A723BA234533012E810)).

The evidence therefore supports a conditional model: closure may make an identity-consistent account easier to seize and defend, but identity, partisanship, and conspiracy mentality may be the more proximate causes. No supplied study directly demonstrates that need for closure mediates a political identity effect on misinformation acceptance.

## 4. Moderators and real-world contexts

### Uncertainty, threat, and crisis

The theoretical case for a closure effect is strongest when uncertainty is costly. Health crises, wars, disasters, elections, and rapidly changing scientific information create precisely the conditions in which people may prefer a coherent answer to a prolonged absence of one.

The Polish COVID-19 study illustrates this setting. Participants were surveyed during the pandemic, and the researchers connected closure subdimensions, conspiracy belief, and coronavirus fear. The study is useful for showing how uncertainty-related motives may become relevant during a crisis, but its snowball sample, mixed outcome measure, and observational design prevent a causal conclusion.

The German panel provides a more demanding test because it measured closure before the pandemic and conspiracy acceptance during it. The positive association remained small, and trust in political and crisis institutions was much stronger. Crucially, neither political trust nor crisis trust moderated the closure relationship. That result weakens a simple account in which closure only matters for people who distrust institutions.

Threat can also have effects that are not specific to misinformation. The threat studies by Thórisdóttir and Jost found increased motivated closed-mindedness, but threat may narrow attention, increase reliance on familiar authorities, heighten group loyalty, or alter political attitudes without producing false beliefs. “Threat increases closure” and “closure increases misinformation acceptance” are separate links, and only the first has clear causal evidence in the supplied sources.

### Partisanship, ideology, and issue involvement

Political identity can change how misinformation is received, but the NFC-specific interaction is largely untested. The Hungarian research found identity-congruent belief in political news, and the broader correction literature shows that politically sophisticated people may defend misinformation when it supports an important attitude. This pattern can occur through motivated reasoning even when a person is capable of careful analysis.

Issue involvement is similarly ambiguous. It can encourage systematic scrutiny because the issue matters, but it can also motivate defense of an existing position. In a U.S. survey experiment on genetically modified food, respondents who considered the issue highly important had higher misinformation scores—2.6 versus 2.3 on a six-point scale among 4,334 adults—but the study controlled need for cognition and a three-item need-for-closure measure rather than estimating a full closure effect. The authors emphasize that importance by itself does not make someone misinformed; false information supporting an important attitude may simply resist change more strongly ([Vidigal and Jerit](https://sites.dartmouth.edu/jerit/files/2022/08/VidigalJerit_PolComm-1.pdf)).

Correction results in that work also varied by fact. In one study, high-importance respondents changed by .55 on a central nutrition fact, compared with .71 among low-importance respondents, but the difference-in-differences was not significant. In another, misinformation fell by 7 percentage points among high-importance respondents and 14 points among low-importance respondents, with a significant difference. These results show why issue importance cannot substitute for need for closure: the same involvement can produce attention, resistance, or both depending on the claim.

There is no comparable direct test of need-for-closure-by-ideology, need-for-closure-by-partisanship, or need-for-closure-by-issue-involvement interactions in the supplied evidence. Any claim that closure effects are uniquely conservative, liberal, partisan, or politically asymmetric would exceed the evidence.

### Source credibility and social cues

Source credibility is a major unresolved boundary. The Hungarian study removed source information, so it cannot answer whether high-closure individuals rely more on familiar institutions, partisan messengers, scientific authorities, or social contacts. The Singapore alert experiment shows that source matters for sharing: participants were less likely to share unfamiliar non-mainstream news overall, but fact-check alerts reduced sharing more for mainstream news. The interpretation was that an alert may violate expectations attached to a reputable source, whereas it may merely confirm low expectations for an unfamiliar one.

This is relevant to need for closure because a credible source can provide a quick basis for certainty. Yet the Singapore study measured sharing likelihood, not belief, and did not measure need for closure. Its result should be treated as a general source-cue boundary, not an NFC moderation finding.

The same caution applies to social endorsement. In the Chinese experiment, social cues affected veracity judgments and engagement. In a different social-media context, reciprocal social ties have been associated with greater acceptance of fact-checks. Such cues may reduce uncertainty for some users and increase distrust for others. Need for closure could plausibly intensify either response, depending on which social source is perceived as authoritative.

### Time pressure, cognitive load, and platform format

The broader misinformation literature indicates that time pressure and cognitive load can reduce discrimination between true and false headlines by increasing belief in false content regardless of political alignment. The 2013 NFCC review also describes time constraints and cognitive load as conditions that can heighten closure. But the combination has rarely been tested directly: the evidence does not show that time pressure increases misinformation specifically by raising need for closure.

Platform context changes the decision environment. A data-donation study of 642 users collected 123,995 Facebook news-related posts and 70,587 off-Facebook news articles over 12 weeks. Misinformation-source exposure was 5.9% of Facebook news exposure compared with 2.6% of off-platform news consumption, while only 4% of off-platform news consumption and 5.7% of off-platform misinformation consumption was driven by Facebook exposure. Several individual differences predicted exposure on Facebook but not deliberate off-platform consumption ([Facebook exposure and off-platform consumption study](https://dl.acm.org/doi/abs/10.1145/3757540)).

Those figures concern exposure and consumption, not belief. Their relevance is that closure may operate differently when a person encounters incidental, rapidly scrolling content than when deliberately seeking information. A cue that is sufficient during a brief feed exposure may be rejected when the person has time to compare sources.

Format also matters. Static headlines, full articles, short videos, community notes, warning labels, and conversational messages create different amounts of time, context, and social pressure. The supplied research does not establish an NFC-by-platform or NFC-by-format interaction.

### Corrections and continued influence

A review of misinformation research proposes that people high in need for closure may trust initial misinformation because it offers a firm explanation and resist a correction because the correction reintroduces uncertainty. This is theoretically coherent, but the review also notes that need for closure is usually included as a control variable and is rarely the main construct. The few direct studies have focused more on endorsement than on correction acceptance ([Social Media and Democracy review](https://www.cambridge.org/core/books/social-media-and-democracy/misinformation-and-its-correction/61FA7FD743784A723BA234533012E810)).

General correction evidence favors explanations that replace a false account rather than merely denying it. A meta-analysis of 20 experiments involving 6,878 participants found that corrections were more effective when they supplied alternative explanations. Another analysis of 30 experiments involving 20,963 participants found weaker fact-checking effects for partial debunks, strongly identified partisans, and false election claims during highly polarized periods. Neither analysis identified need for closure as a moderator ([correction evidence synthesis](https://arxiv.org/html/2206.15237v1)).

The distinction between an alternative explanation and a bare denial is especially relevant to closure. A bare “that is false” may leave an explanatory gap. A concise account of what happened, why it happened, and how the evidence supports that account can provide a new basis for certainty. This is a reason to expect detailed corrections to help high-closure recipients, but it is not evidence that they do so more than other recipients.

There is also no NFC-specific evidence on prebunking, debunking, or continued influence. Reviews distinguish initial belief from the persistence of misinformation’s influence after correction, and the supplied studies do not show whether closure affects one, the other, or neither. A person may accept a correction while still using the old claim in an inference task, or may reject a claim initially but later rely on it through familiarity.

### Does closure selectively increase misinformation acceptance?

The evidence cannot answer this question decisively. A selective effect would require showing that high closure increases acceptance of false information more than acceptance of true information, ideally while measuring both direct belief and discrimination. The supplied studies do not provide such a test.

The Hungarian study examined both fake and real political news and found no adjusted closure signal for either outcome. The illusory-truth program found no closure moderation of a general repetition effect. The German study measured conspiracy claims without a comparable set of true claims. Hejniak et al. studied misleading details in a memory task without a direct true-versus-false credibility comparison.

The most defensible interpretation is that need for closure may affect information processing generally—especially the speed of commitment, cue use, and revision—rather than creating a misinformation-specific deficit. A selective misinformation effect remains possible, but it is not demonstrated.

## 5. Comparison with related psychological predictors

Need for closure is easiest to misunderstand when it is treated as a general label for all forms of closed-minded or nonanalytic thinking. Several neighboring constructs overlap with it but answer different questions.

| Construct | Core question | What the evidence suggests | Distinctive limitation |
|---|---|---|---|
| Need for closure | How strongly does someone want uncertainty settled? | May promote rapid commitment and freezing when ambiguity is costly | Does not specify whether the settled answer is true or false |
| Need for cognition | How much does someone enjoy and seek effortful thinking? | Relates to engagement with complex material | Is not the opposite of need for closure |
| Analytic thinking or CRT | Does someone override an intuitive response and inspect evidence? | Often predicts better true–false discernment | Performance and disposition are not identical to closure motivation |
| Intolerance of ambiguity or uncertainty | How uncomfortable is an unclear situation? | Overlaps with closure, especially during threat | Does not necessarily include the urgency to adopt and preserve an answer |
| Conspiracy mentality | How readily does someone interpret events through hidden coordinated actors? | More consistently associated with fake-news belief in some studies | Is a content-related belief tendency, not merely a motive to end uncertainty |
| Epistemic vice or intellectual humility | Does someone disregard evidence or recognize fallibility? | Epistemic vice can strongly predict misinformation; humility can protect against belief and sharing | Neither is interchangeable with need for closure |

### Need for cognition is not the opposite of need for closure

The Need for Cognition Scale measures the tendency to engage in and enjoy effortful cognitive activity. Need for closure measures the desire for a definite answer instead of confusion and ambiguity ([construct comparison](https://doi.org/10.1177/01461672231154886)). A person could enjoy analyzing information while still wanting the analysis to end in a firm conclusion. Conversely, someone could dislike effortful thinking but tolerate uncertainty rather than quickly commit.

This distinction explains why the two constructs should not be placed on a single “thinking hard versus thinking lazily” continuum. Klein and Webster’s finding that high-closure participants processed systematically when no heuristic cue was available is direct evidence against equating closure with an inability to reason.

### Analytic thinking and actively open-minded thinking

Analytic thinking concerns the capacity or disposition to override an intuitive response and examine evidence. In two studies with 1,973 Americans, analytic thinking was generally associated with better discrimination between true and false or hyperpartisan headlines and was not associated with reduced discernment ([Ross, Rand, and Pennycook](https://www.sas.upenn.edu/~baron/journal/20/200616b/jdm200616b.html)).

Actively open-minded thinking goes further by emphasizing willingness to consider alternative explanations, revise beliefs, and follow evidence even when it conflicts with one’s initial position. Research summarized in the four-component thinking-style program reports that actively open-minded thinking outperformed the Cognitive Reflection Test in predicting COVID-19 misperceptions and discernment of true and false vaccination news ([Newton, Feeney, and Pennycook](https://doi.org/10.1177/01461672231154886)). A 2025 validation found that open-minded and close-minded thinking styles predicted unfounded beliefs, but also emphasized conceptual and psychometric problems in measuring these styles ([Ballová Mikušková et al.](https://doi.org/10.1177/01461672251327607)).

These findings make analytic and open-minded thinking plausible predictors of accuracy, but they do not establish that need for closure adds independent predictive power. No supplied study reports a comparable same-sample incremental coefficient for closure against need for cognition, CRT, actively open-minded thinking, intolerance of uncertainty, dogmatism, and conspiracy mentality.

### Intolerance of ambiguity is related but not identical

Intolerance of ambiguity describes discomfort with situations that have multiple interpretations or incomplete information. Need for closure includes that discomfort but adds a motivational preference to seize and preserve a definite answer. The German study explicitly distinguishes closure from traits such as intolerance of ambiguity and dogmatism, describing closure as the cognitive-motivational dynamic underlying epistemic needs for certainty ([Jedinger and Masch](https://www.frontiersin.org/journals/social-psychology/articles/10.3389/frsps.2024.1447313/full)).

This distinction matters empirically. Someone may dislike ambiguity but remain undecided while gathering evidence. Someone high in closure may move beyond discomfort and adopt whichever explanation resolves the uncertainty. Short scales that combine ambiguity discomfort, decisiveness, and closed-mindedness can blur these cases.

### Conspiracy mentality may be closer to the outcome

Conspiracy mentality is a general tendency to perceive important events as the product of hidden, coordinated actors. Unlike need for closure, it contains more directional content: the preferred answer often involves secret plots, powerful groups, or intentional deception.

In the Hungarian fake-news study, conspiracy mentality was the only psychological predisposition consistently related to belief in political and nonpolitical fake news after adjustment. In the U.S. study of 998 adults, the Epistemic Vice Scale correlated *r* = .76 with COVID-19 misinformation acceptance, while the Cognitive Reflection Test correlated *r* = −.39. Adding epistemic-vice subscales increased explained variance by ΔR² = .09; the supplied results do not provide the need-for-closure coefficient ([Meyer, Alfano, and de Bruin](https://doi.org/10.1017/epi.2021.18)).

The comparison does not prove that conspiracy mentality or epistemic vice always matters more than closure. It does show that a broad certainty motive may be less proximal than a specific suspicion of authorities, indifference to evidence, or rigidity about belief. Treating all of these as “closed-mindedness” would conceal meaningful differences.

### Dogmatism, closed-mindedness, and intellectual humility

Need for closure is correlated with dogmatism and closed-mindedness, but it is not reducible to either. The Turkish scale work is informative because closed-mindedness items were removed while the core certainty-and-clarity factor remained. This suggests that a need to settle uncertainty can be measured without assuming that the person refuses every alternative idea.

Intellectual humility represents a contrasting disposition: awareness that one’s intuitions may be fallible and that other people may possess relevant knowledge. Across three U.S. surveys involving 4,800 partisan participants, intellectual humility was reported to protect against both believing and sharing hostile false political news. That evidence does not estimate need for closure, but it identifies a different route to misinformation resistance ([moralization and intellectual humility study](https://doi.org/10.1080/10584609.2024.2363542)).

The incremental role of need for closure therefore remains unsettled. It may explain when people stop searching, whereas conspiracy mentality explains what kind of explanation they prefer, analytic thinking explains whether they inspect evidence, and intellectual humility explains whether they remain open to correction. Direct comparisons are needed before any of these constructs can be treated as substitutes.

## 6. Limitations, implications, and bottom line

### Measurement limits

The first limitation is construct measurement. Studies use different versions of the NFCS, from 15 items to five, and some combine dimensions that may have different relations to misinformation. In the Polish COVID-19 study, the ambiguity-avoidance and closed-mindedness subscales had α values of .56 and .59. In the German panel, the five-item measure had α = .67. Low reliability generally attenuates associations, but short scales can also make it unclear which aspect of closure is responsible for a result.

Median splits create another problem. Hejniak et al. classified people as high or low closure using a median split, which discards information and can make groups appear more distinct than the underlying continuous relationship. A continuous, preregistered model would provide a more stable test.

Measurement equivalence is also incomplete across cultures. The cross-cultural validation supports a common structure but only partial metric and scalar invariance. A score difference between countries may therefore reflect item interpretation, response style, or cultural meanings of decisiveness rather than a genuine difference in the psychological motive.

Outcome measurement is equally important. Many studies use agreement or likelihood ratings in online surveys. The U.S. COVID-19 study explicitly cautions that its instrument cannot distinguish belief from credence, confidence, or suspended judgment. A person selecting “probably true” may be endorsing a claim, guessing, signaling uncertainty, or responding expressively. Sharing intention is another step removed from belief, and actual sharing is another step removed from both.

### Causal and generalizability limits

The central causal limitation is the absence of a direct randomized test of need for closure and misinformation acceptance. Trait studies cannot rule out political trust, conspiracy mentality, education, media exposure, cognitive ability, or other correlated variables. Temporal separation in the German panel improves the design but does not establish that closure caused later conspiracy belief.

The available state evidence is adjacent rather than decisive. Threat manipulations increase motivated closed-mindedness, and accountability may reduce the influence of prior conspiracy beliefs, but neither design directly manipulates closure while measuring a standardized misinformation outcome. The supplied evidence does not establish a causal NFC effect on sharing or correction acceptance.

Samples and contexts also vary widely. Positive results come from young Polish participants, Polish online volunteers, and a representative German panel. Null findings come from Hungarian social-media volunteers, a small British student sample, and a seven-study repetition program using mostly experimental participants. COVID-19 dominates the recent literature, while ordinary political, financial, scientific, and interpersonal misinformation receive less direct NFC testing. Research is also concentrated in the United States and Europe, with less harmonized evidence from other regions.

Ecological validity is limited by memory films, balanced headline sets, hypothetical claims, static screenshots, and short online tasks. A person judging a headline in a survey is not necessarily behaving like someone who encounters a claim in a social network, sees a friend endorse it, and decides whether to forward it. Platform data show that exposure, deliberate consumption, belief, and sharing are different stages, but they do not yet connect those stages to closure.

### Practical implications

The first implication is caution against labeling high-closure people as inherently gullible. Need for closure can make a person settle quickly, but it does not specify which answer will be accepted. It may encourage reliance on a trustworthy source, a well-supported explanation, or an accurate correction just as it may encourage reliance on a misleading cue.

Communication should therefore reduce unnecessary ambiguity without pretending that complex evidence is simpler than it is. A correction that explains what happened, why the false claim is wrong, and what evidence supports the alternative is more likely to provide a usable replacement account than a bare denial. This recommendation follows general correction evidence, not an NFC-specific intervention test.

The second implication concerns credibility. Corrections should come from sources that the relevant audience regards as competent and legitimate, while acknowledging that source effects can be politically and culturally conditional. The Singapore experiment found that fact-check alerts reduced sharing, but the effect differed by source and did not necessarily imply a change in belief. The 2025 warning-tag study suggests that closure may affect attitudes toward interventions, but it does not yet show which warning design works best for high-closure recipients.

The third implication is to separate interventions by outcome. A warning may reduce sharing without changing belief. A detailed correction may reduce direct belief while leaving claim-congruent inferences or continued influence. Prebunking may affect later judgments differently from reactive debunking. Research and policy evaluations should measure credibility, direct belief, confidence, true–false discrimination, inference, recall, sharing, and correction acceptance separately.

Accuracy prompts and modest sharing friction are reasonable general strategies because misinformation often spreads when users act quickly. But there is no evidence that a particular prompt, warning label, or correction format has been tested specifically for people high in need for closure. Tailoring interventions to that group should remain an empirical question, not a settled recommendation.

### Bottom line

Need for closure is best understood as a possible amplifier of rapid commitment and cue reliance under uncertainty, not as a general misinformation trait. Small positive associations have appeared in a Polish memory paradigm and a German study of COVID-19 conspiracy beliefs. Counterevidence includes an adjusted Hungarian null result, near-zero British correlations, and the absence of need-for-closure moderation in a seven-study illusory-truth program.

The evidence supports moderate confidence that closure motives can contribute to misinformation acceptance in ambiguous, threatening, or cue-rich settings. Confidence is low that need for closure alone causes acceptance, selectively increases false rather than true beliefs, increases sharing, or produces resistance to corrections. The most accurate answer is therefore conditional: need for closure may help determine how quickly people settle on an explanation, but what they settle on depends heavily on source credibility, identity, trust, familiarity, issue involvement, available alternatives, and the quality of corrective information.
